by.claim: Tock timekeeping records — the underlying support for 'actual time and material costs' billed to federal partners under signed IAAs — cannot show who actually authored a given entry: when the Tock team enters hours on behalf of an absent employee, 'the timesheet has no field for who submitted the entry, so an entry made by the Tock team and an entry made by the employee are the same record afterwards,' and the timekeeping manager's weekly check only confirms a timecard exists, not who filed it. Because 18F represents these hours to client agencies as the employee's actual billable time (per the IAA billing and monthly-accounting terms), a record whose authorship cannot be reconstructed creates exposure if a client or auditor later challenges the accuracy of a specific charge.

State/local IGCA request letters may be signed by a delegated official instead of the chief executive, but the underlying delegation or authorizing statute is only orally 'confirmed' by the account manager — 'the instrument itself is not collected, and it is not one of the items assembled into the package that goes for review and signature.' Every other IAA/IGCA component (SOW, cost estimate, advance payment waiver) is expressly routed through the Agreements Team and OGC review before execution, but the one document that would prove the signer had authority to bind the state or city is never captured in the record OGC reviews, leaving the agreement's enforceability against the non-federal partner resting on an unverified, undocumented assertion.
